question: Can a tiny Transformer trained only on local one- and two-column addition transitions be reused recurrently to add numbers far longer than any training sequence?

key_findings.claim: Training examples factor addition into two finite transition types: add a pair of digits, or add the next digit pair conditioned on the previous local output and carry.
key_findings.evidence: Section 2 defines a 14-token vocabulary and examples such as 69 to 15S and 15C29 to 12S. Inputs and targets are padded to fixed lengths five and three, so the learned mapping is a bounded local transition.

key_findings.claim: A two-layer, 64-dimensional decoder-only Transformer with two attention heads and a 256-dimensional feed-forward block learns this local transition under ordinary Adam training.
key_findings.evidence: Section 3 specifies the architecture, modified attention mask, learning rate 5e-4, weight decay 0.01, 20% dropout, and batch size 512.

key_findings.claim: An external autoregressive controller applies the bounded learned transition from least to most significant column and assembles the last digits into the final answer.
key_findings.evidence: Section 4 walks through 65785+8765 as five separate model calls and specifies a deterministic collation rule. The model never attends over either complete long operand in one forward pass.

anchors.section: Section 4, token generation and worked example

key_findings.claim: The implementation reportedly gets every one of more than 1,000 sampled additions up to 1,000 digits correct and also succeeds on selected operands up to 300,000 digits.
key_findings.evidence: Section 4.1 reports no errors in those tests but does not provide a per-length sample table, confidence bound, adversarial carry-chain suite, or independent replication.

key_findings.claim: The title's arbitrary-length Transformer generalization is operationally a learned finite-state digit adder embedded in a hand-coded loop, not one Transformer forward pass generalizing its attention or position representation to arbitrary sequence length.
key_findings.evidence: Training and inference always present at most five input tokens to the model; length is handled entirely by repeated calls and deterministic carry/result bookkeeping. The paper itself states that the model handles at most two single digits at a time.

method.core_idea: Learn the constant-size transition rule for one addition column and compose that rule an arbitrary number of times outside the Transformer.
method.mechanism: Generate local training pairs with and without carry context, train a tiny decoder on fixed-size sequences, traverse operands right-to-left at inference, feed each column and previous local output back into the model, and concatenate returned digits deterministically.
assumptions: Base-10 two-operand addition is exactly representable by a finite carry state.
The model learns all relevant local digit/carry cases rather than a brittle subset.
An external controller may perform segmentation, recurrence, padding, and output assembly.

techniques.role: Reduces unbounded addition to a finite supervised table.
Composes the learned map over arbitrary operand length.
Builds the global result from local predictions.

evaluations.setting: More than 1,000 randomly sampled two-operand additions with up to 1,000 digits
evaluations.result: The paper reports 100% accuracy on all sampled cases.
evaluations.baseline: Exact integer addition computed by the test script

evaluations.setting: Selected additions with operands extending to 300,000 digits
evaluations.result: The paper reports positive results on all attempted tests but gives no sample count or runtime curve.

limitations: No comparative baseline, per-length accuracy table, multiple-seed study, or statistical interval is reported.
The recurrent controller encodes most of the known addition algorithm and constrains the learned task to a finite local map.
Inference requires one model call per digit column and runtime scaling is not measured.
Only two-operand base-10 addition is evaluated; transfer to harder algorithms is speculative.
The very large-digit tests are described informally and limited by compute.
failure_modes: A rare local transition error propagates through later carry states and corrupts the full suffix.
A different tokenizer, radix, signed-number convention, or operand count invalidates the handcrafted state representation.
Adversarial all-nine carry chains may expose local cases underrepresented in random testing.
Autoregressive error probability accumulates approximately with the number of model calls.
reusable_insights: Factor an algorithm into a minimal bounded transition and test local completeness before claiming length generalization.
Distinguish model-internal sequence generalization from algorithmic composition supplied by an external controller.
Report adversarial transition coverage and end-to-end error scaling, not only randomly sampled perfect accuracy.
open_questions: Can the local transition be formally verified over all digit and carry cases?
How does end-to-end reliability scale to millions of recurrent calls under stochastic decoding or quantization?
Which less obviously finite-state tasks can be learned with similarly minimal external scaffolding?

competitive_landscape.title: Teaching Arithmetic to Small Transformers
competitive_landscape.difference: Lee et al. study next-token arithmetic, formatting, sample complexity, and chain-of-thought; this paper instead trains a fixed local carry transition and composes model calls externally.

competitive_landscape.title: Transformers Can Do Arithmetic with the Right Embeddings
competitive_landscape.relationship: Addition length generalization through positional structure
competitive_landscape.difference: The Abacus-style approach processes full operand sequences and improves extrapolation with digit-position embeddings; this paper keeps every learned input fixed-length and delegates global recurrence to code.

competitive_landscape.title: Position Coupling: Improving Length Generalization of Arithmetic Transformers Using Task Structure
competitive_landscape.difference: Position Coupling aligns equal-significance digits inside one Transformer sequence and gives a one-layer construction; this method removes long positions altogether through a recurrent local interface.

competitive_landscape.title: Arithmetic Transformers Can Length-Generalize in Both Operand Length and Count
competitive_landscape.difference: The later work tackles simultaneous operand-length and operand-count extrapolation with scratchpads and multi-level position coupling; the reviewed system handles only two operands with a hard-coded per-column loop.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: Representative local training instances let a tiny Transformer trained on two-digit addition generalize perfectly to arbitrary operand lengths without a scratchpad.
novelty_assessment.evidence: A reproducible R implementation reports no failures in over 1,000 additions up to 1,000 digits and selected much longer cases.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: The useful result is reliable learned finite-state composition. It should not be conflated with a Transformer itself extrapolating attention across arbitrary input lengths, and the perfect-accuracy claim needs exhaustive local verification and stronger end-to-end testing.

reviewer_notes: Read all 8 pages, checking every training-instance type, architecture setting, recurrent inference rule, empirical claim, limitation, and reference. Current arithmetic competitors were checked on arXiv on 2026-08-23.
